title: Contortionism: Bend It Like Gumby
summary: Josh and Chuck explore contortionism, from ancient depictions in Syria, Egypt, Greece, China, and India through 17th-18th century English "posture masters" and the circus era, to Mongolia as its modern center (Mongolian State Circus, contortion schools, the Buddhist Somme dance, and the bid for UNESCO heritage protection that was rejected in 2011). They cover basic backbend and front bend moves, advanced feats like the Marinelli bend, genetic conditions linked to hypermobility (EDS, Marfan syndrome, the Beighton scale), training methods such as PNF stretching, and the myotatic reflex. The episode ends with a listener email praising the show.
topics: stuff you should know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and episode title
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on contortionism and the listener-suggested title 'Bend It Like Gumby.'

segments.title: Ancient origins of contortionism
segments.summary: Earliest likely depiction of a contortionist from Syria around 2300 BCE with swords, Hittite writings describing sword-hoop performances, Egyptian pottery from about 1200 BCE showing backbends, Greek performers, and Chinese contortionists possibly influenced by Europe.

segments.title: Contortion in India and yoga
segments.summary: Indian temple sculptures from the tenth century CE show contorted poses; the discussion touches on Kama Sutra poses, tantric practice, and links between contortion and yoga.

segments.title: English posture masters
segments.summary: In 17th and 18th century England, male posture masters performed contortion in public, sometimes busking; Joseph Clark was a famous contortionist whose name became shorthand for the act.

segments.title: Contortion in the circus
segments.summary: Philip and Patty Astley's late 18th century circus spread to the US; the term contortionist arrived around 1860, performers often claimed foreign identities, and women came to dominate the act for male audiences. Nna Bertoldi toured from age eight and was filmed by Edison's kinetoscope.

segments.title: Transition to Mongolia
segments.summary: Hosts tease that Mongolia is the epicenter of contortionism before a break.

segments.title: Mongolia as the center of contortion
segments.summary: Mongolia's contortion tradition is tied to meditative practice and the Buddhist Somme dance, and to the indigenous folk dance Bilge. Twelfth-century growth, a seventeenth-century Buddhist leader who inspired sculptures of contorted poses, and Soviet-era state funding through the Mongolian State Circus made it world renowned, with many contortion schools following.

segments.title: Decline of Mongolian contortion and UNESCO bid
segments.summary: Mongolian contortion is declining in distinctiveness as trainers go abroad and schools multiply; the country sought UNESCO intangible heritage status, which UNESCO rejected in 2011.

segments.title: UNESCO heritage follow-up
segments.summary: Hosts note the Bilge folk dance is protected by UNESCO and Josh says he will look into UNESCO heritage rejections for a future short stuff episode.

segments.title: Basic backbends and contortion moves
segments.summary: The hosts describe the chest stand, front bend, and the difficulty of describing these poses; they discuss how the transitions between poses matter, and the balancing and feats of strength used in circus acts.

segments.title: Advanced tricks: Marinelli bend, shoulder pass-through, splits, spinal twisting
segments.summary: The Marinelli bend is a chest stand supported by the teeth; Mongolian contortionist Sastral Ordenablig holds the record at four minutes seventeen seconds. Other moves include the shoulder pass-through, splits and over splits, standing splits, and vertebra-by-vertebra twisting.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the discussion of the darker side of contortion.

segments.title: Hypermobility and genetic conditions
segments.summary: Double jointedness is really hypermobility, rated on the Beighton scale up to nine. Genetic conditions such as Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (thirteen types affecting connective tissue) can correlate with extreme flexibility; contortion is not linked to a higher injury rate or shorter life, and the old belief that contortionists die young may stem from early career exits.

segments.title: Hormones, Marfan syndrome, and health tradeoffs
segments.summary: Progestin-only birth control may increase hypermobility; Marfan syndrome causes flexibility plus heart and breathing issues; hypermobility spectrum disorder is an umbrella term. Studies found contortionists' bodies are not unusual, including MRI findings.

segments.title: Training to become a contortionist
segments.summary: Training usually starts in childhood because of greater flexibility; professionals train for hours daily with strength work. The myotatic reflex limits normal stretching, so PNF stretches are used to lengthen muscle fibers. Water intake and gradual neural and pain-tolerance adaptations are also discussed.

segments.title: Seeing contortionists live
segments.summary: Hosts discuss seeing contortionists in person, with Circa Solei mentioned, and suggest a family outing.

segments.title: Listener email: top ten compliments
segments.summary: Listener Sarah sends a list of compliments about the show's intro banter, episode titles, recipes, kindness, personal openness, informative topics, the intro and outro music, mispronunciations and accents, kid-friendly listening, and the Madison tour dates.
